speechtext:
1.	What is the custom of the Department of Public Printing and Stationery in issuing the blank ballots used in the Dominion elections ? How many ballots are contained on each sheet of paper ?
2.	Is the paper on which the ballots are printed issued direct from the Printing Bureau to the several returning officers throughout Canada, or does it go through the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery ?
3.	Are the sheets of ballot paper carefully counted before being sent out, and Is a record kept of the number of sheets sent to each returning officer ? If so, under whose supervision was this done ?
4.	After the issue of the sheets of ballot paper to the several returning officers for the last Dominion elections, wras any complaint made to the Department of Public Printing and Stationery, or to the Clerk of the Crown In Chancery, by any returning officer, or by his subordinates, or by any printing establishment, that' the requisite number of sheets of paper for such constituency or constituencies had not been furnished, or that the actual number of sheets was less than that which the returning officer was credited with having received ?
5.	If so, in what constituency or constituencies did this occur, and what action was taken on such complaint ?

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext:
1.	The main principles are :	(a) To deal
with no one but returning officers, (d) To have no broken packages. The ballots are issued in sheets of 4 and 2 according to the sample which I lay on the table.
2.	The ballots are issued direct from the Printing Bureau to the returning officers throughout Canada without the intervention of tlie Clerk of the Crown iu Chancery.
3.	The sheets are carefully counted before being packed. They are sent out in closed packages of three sizes only, viz : Packages of 2,000 in fours and of 1,000 and of 500 in twos. The packages are not opened after being counted. The smaller packages are used for uneven or broken thousands. The counting is done in the bindery, after cutting, by skilled bauds aud under the supervision of tlie foreman of the bindery. The packages are then finally closed and pasted up.
4.	After the issue of the ballots, applications were received by the King's Printer from returning officers where the supply was insuificieut. In all such cases the additional ballots required by the returning officer were sent to him, but always in whole packages. No ballots whatever were sent to any printing office but they were sent cut iu sealed bags by registered post to the returning officers. No communications from others than returning officers were entertained.
speakername: Right Hon. Sir WILFRID LAURIER (Prime Minister):

They provide a daily service between the points mentioned and a full round trip and they carry the mails.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Has the department any proposals with regard to putting on a new boat and increasing the subsidy?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Communications have passed between the company and the department and they are under consideration, but no change is involved in the vote now asked for. If another boat were put on or a new contract made, it would be necessary, I think, to have a supplementary vote.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Is the contract renewed?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I suppose the contract could be renewed during the summer.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
I may state that the Board of Trade of Charlottetown passed a resolution complaining of the high rates which shippers and passengers have to pay on these boats. They also complain that while the company has a very good boat on the Summerside route, the ' Princess', which at present runs between Charlottetown and Pictou, is one which has outlasted her usefulness to a great extent, and that the large increase of trade between those two points require a much larger boat. I understand Hat the company are willing to put on a much larger boat, but they cannot do it with the subsidy now given. I notice that the subsidy immediately preceding this one, for communication between the mainland and the Magdalen Islands, amounts to $15,000. I am not complaining of that, but the minister and the House know that the service between Prince Edward Island and the mainland is one which the Dominion government is pledged by the terms of confederation to maintain, and the sums voted for it are ridiculously small. This steam navigation company has done a great service to the province, but the accommodation at Charlottetown at present is not equal to what the public demands. I may say that the freight on 100 lbs. of goods of the first class from St. John, N.B., to Sydney, a distance of 400 miles, is only 30c, whereas the rate from St. John to Charlottetown, a distance of only 190 miles, is 59c. This large rate is to a great extent owing to the heavy freights charged by this company, but the company says there is no remedy unless the subsidy is increased. I hope, therefore,

that when the supplementary estimates come down there will be a further vote to increase this subsidy. The trade between the province and the mainland is rapidly increasing, and it requires much better accommodation than is at present provided, especially between Charlottetown and Pic-tou.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
With inference to the request of my hon. friend from Queen's, I would like to point out that there is one condition in regard to this proposed vote which seems to be applicable to every proposition that relates to communication between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. That is the proposition that these boats and services should be conducted entirely in the interests of Prince Edward Island, and for the sole benefit of the people of that province. I may say that those who are interested in the company which owns the boats for which this vote has been given belong entirely to Prince Edward Island. My hon. friend is quite right in stating that the service is inefficient, and that the boat now running between Charlottetown and Pictou is not at all satisfactory or fitted to cope with the large trade which has grown up and the passenger traffic between the two points. But this company has earn-' ed large dividends and has a large amount at rest, which it proposes to utilize for the purpose of obtaining a new boat; and those who live on the mainland and have occasion sometimes to visit this garden of the gulf would like to see these gentlemen who own the boats which are earning these large dividends run them with some consideration for the requirements of the people who have not the advantage of living in that favoured locality, and the government should see that they do so before granting any further favours. Should any one who happens to live on the mainland desire to visit the island, he cannot do so in less than three days, both going and returning, no matter from what part of Nova Scotia he may start. Therefore, before this company is given the slightest increase of subsidy, the government should see that it runs its boats from Charlottetown to Pictou in such a way that people living in Nova Scotia will be able to go to Charlottetown and return within twenty-four hours at least. There is no particular reason why that should not be done, and no reason why the population in Nova Scotia and the maritime provinces generally should not receive some attention from the management of this service. I need hardly remind my hon. friend that this particular company, not so very long ago, was very active in opposing before this parliament a proposition to give another company a charter to engage in this same service ; and I am therefore not asking anything unreasonable when I ask that the government shall insist, before giving this company any additional subsidy or renewal
of contract on its placing upon the route between Charlottetown and Pictou a larger and more commodious steamer than the one it has at present. And further, that this company should be compelled to so arrange the sailings of its boats that it would be possible for any one to leave Pictou in the morning and go to Charlottetown and return at night, instead of following the present system of having both boats leave the island in the morning, thus rendering it impossible for any one to get to and fro in any period less than three days.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend that when the government subsidizes these boats their hours of sailing should be subject to -the approval of the government. The allegation that the company is very wealthy, is one that is considerably disputed, and I am not aware that it is a matter of record that it has a large rest. If any company in Nova Scotia is ready to take hold of the service, there is nothing to prevent their getting to work ; but hitherto the boat on the Summerside route has given every satisfaction, although I must say that the boat on the route between Charlottetown and Pictou is not at all adequate for the traffic, and should be replaced by a better one. Whether or not the service can be performed with the present subsidy is very doubtful, especially if the freights are kept as low as they are on other routes. We contend that the rates from any point in Canada to any point in Charlottetown should not exceed any charged on the Intercolonial Railway in other parts of Canada. Prince Edward Island has suffered extremely in that respect. The freights on those boats are extremely high. Whether that be due to the fact that the subsidy is not large enough, is one on which I am not prepared to express an opinion, but the subsidy is certainly not large. I see that we give a much larger subsidy to the service to Magdalen Island. I hope, however, that the hon. minister will see that some improvement is effected, and that is the only reason why I call his attention to the matter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
I take it that no fault was found with the steamer which runs between Summerside and .Point Du Chene. which makes fifteen knots an hour, but that it is the boat which runs between Pictou and Charlottetown, that only makes twelve knots an hour, that is complained of.
Steam communication from July 1st, 1905, to June 30th, 1906, between Grand Manan and the mainland, $5,000.

speechtext: There is no change in that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Speaking generally with regard to all these boats, what attention does the Department of Trade and Commerce give to these different carriers so as to be informed whether they are really of service, whether their trade is increasing, and what value they are giving for the money. Some of these are valuable because communication should be kept up between the points. But most of these subsidies are paid because they are in aid of trade and commerce. A number of years ago, we made a very careful revision of the subsidies paid, and considerable changes were made. A number were cut off as not being useful, some were reduced, some were increased, and one or two new ones put on in the places of those cut off. That is, we thought it well to take stock and see whether we were paying money where there was no adequate return to the public. The list is largely increasing, I find. We are paying here $968 -000-practically a million dollars in subsidies for services across the Atlantic, to West India and on local routes. I suppose the* Trade and Commerce Department in some way gets at the facts with reference to these services, the volume of trade and the increase or decrease in that volume, in order that it may know whether it is right to continue or discontinue the service, or whether it would be better to increase the subsidy- because it is evidently poor policy to pay a certain amount for an inferior service if, by doubling the payment, you can secure an adequate service and increase trade between the ports touched at. Is there any system of gathering information which could serve the department and the House in judging as to the usefulnesss of these subsidies, which of them are paying, what future there is for each and, where a service is not really effective, what means would be taken to improve it ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
I understand from the deputy of the department that reports are received, but I do not know that they cover the information referred to. I suppose the contract provides for the carrying out of certain considerations, and this is done. But I gather that the only other information is in the form of complaints from parties who object that the contracts are not carried Mr. PATERSON.
out. I understand the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) to ask if there is any systematic report from which the House could judge whether the subsidy has been effective in promoting trade. I understand that there are no such reports.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Would it not be a good idea for the government, through some minister, to make a statement reviewing this whole vote, so that the House and the country might be able to judge whether it is conferring any benefit. If this cannot be done this year it should be understood that the government will be prepared next year to justify these votes or to suggest some improvement. An expenditure so great as this should certainly be reviewed on the basis of information by the House, that the public may know whether they are getting any thing for their money.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I may supplement what I said by what the deputy minister now tells me. It does not contradict what I said before but adds to it. Before payment is made the customs officers and postal authorities have to sign certificates that the work imposed by the contract has been properly performed. That, of course, does not necessarily affect the question of increase in internal commerce through the subsidy. It does show that there is some supervision and that subsidies are not paid with out assurance that the service has been performed. But I do not think there is any information before the department bearing upon the question of the effect of these subsidies in increasing trade.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: That, however, is the important part of it. Subsidies were given first in iiopes of developing trade by that means. I know that, in some cases, the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated to the House that the subsidy was given in anticipation of developing a good trade. If it is found that trade cannot be developed by this means, it would be wise to stop the subsidy. There should be some data presented to the House to enable it to judge of the usefulness of these subsidies, and so to justify our action in voting them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
The minister will see that the supervision he speaks of is merely mechanical supervision. Certificates are demanded showing that certain trips were made. But whether the vessel sailed light cr full laden is not shown. I make the suggestion I do because I think if it were carried out it would help in the intelligent consideration of this question. And the question must be considered sooner or later, because the country will not go on voting a million dollars for steamship services without demanding to know whether value is received or not. Demands are coming in for new services, and, as all demands cannot be met, we must judge for which our money should be spent. There are custom house

officers who could give information, and the officers of the vessels themselves could return the volume of trade from year to year and also the kind of trade, which would be valuable information for the House to have as showing the development of the inter-port commerce of the country. The minister said that complaints have been made as to some of these services. I suppose these complaints have been investigated. If not, they ought to be. Then, by simple process of reporting in answer to questions framed and sent out by the department to the proper officers of the government and of the vessels themselves, much information could be gathered. If that has not been done, I hope that before next year it will be done, for we must look at these things from a business point of view and not give subsidies simply because certain persons ask for them, but because they are in the public interest.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: The steamer that performs this service was equipped specially for this route and this purpose, and I presume that she was built of such a size and character as would enable her adequately to perform the service expected of her.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Speaking individually, it seems to me that the remarks of the member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) are very practical, and I do not see that it is at all an impossible thing to get what he requires. Also speaking personally, and with such knowledge as I have, I should think it would be very important that we should have that information. Is it wise to keep this thing on at all ? On the other hand, if the traffic is greatly increased, do they require as much subsidy as they are getting ? I think the observation is a practical one, and well worthy of consideration, and I have no doubt it will be brought to the minister's attention through the ' Hansard.' Further than that, I cannot say, but it seems to me it is a practical suggestion, and that some way ought to be found of carrying it out.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
Is not that the very work this Department of Trade and Commerce was created for ? Some years ago a new department called the Department of Trade and Commerce was created at a large expense, and a minister was put in charge of it, and this matter especially was one of those to come under his control. The hon. gentleman in assuming a responsibility of that kind should be prepared to justify all these expenditures, and to give a general report and review of the situation. I hope that next year, if not this year, parliament will be given some information from the Minister of Trade and Commerce in regard to this very item. It is a large item, and concerns the development of our trade, and we ought to have some report from him showing whether the money we are spending is developing our trade or not.

speechtext: That touches at a great many ports. The vessel is the ' Gas-pesia', of 490 tons gross, and 287 tons net, ICO feet long by 27 feet broad.

As the hon. gentleman knows, there is no communication from Summit or Metis, on the Intercolonial with the other side of the peninsula, as far as Paspebiac. It is a mountainous region, and there are several little coves on the coast, and settlements of

fishermen, who now can send their fish to Quebec, Montreal and other places by this boat.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: What general work does a boat like that do ?

speechtext: vVhat is the distance ?

speechtext: I think it is something like 800 miles.

speechtext:
How many knots ?
Mr. LEMIEUa. About 11 knots.

(Mr. ANGUS A. McLEAN. I think this service could be greatly improved. maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I believe only $2,500 were paid last year, because they had not carried out the full requirements of the contract.

speechtext: Shippers in Prince Edward Island are anxious to obtain boats under the contract to run to Liverpool as that market suits most of them better than Manchester. Is it the intention of the government to arrange for such a service ?

speechtext: The subject is under consideration, I am told, now, a decision not having yet been arrived at. The parties who had the contract before were the Manchester Liners, Limited. maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: The hon. minister ought to give some reason why they did not make both trips.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I understand that during 1903, only $1,500 was paid for one trip. Why should they be paid $2,500 for the same service last year ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.

Mi'. INGRAM. Do I understand the hon. minister to say that $7,000 was voted last year and that only $2,500 was expended?

speechtext:
Last year, $7,000 was placed in the estimates in the expectation that there would be a larger number of trips between the province of Prince Edward Island and Great Britain than formerly. Any person can understand that one trip between Prince Edward Island and Great Britain is not what the province should have. In the production of cattle, sheep, bacon, ham, eggs, butter and cheese, there is no similar area in the Dominion of Canada that can equal the province of Prince Edward Island and without adequate shipping facilities the farmers are very much handicapped. We know very well now that Great Britain is our market but what position is Prince Edward Island in ? The first thing that our exporters have to do is to ship their goods to Halifax and then tranship them to the vessel from Halifax to the old country. Thus they are handicapped in every way, and I think that in place of having one trip per annum Prince Edward Island should have at least seven trips. Every time that the boat did come to the port at Charlottetown she could nbt accommodate all the freight that was offered, and the cold storage accommodation was not at all sufficient, and yet they think they are doing a great deal for Prince Edward. Island by giving one trip per annum. trips are provided for this service he would he doing an immense service for the province. speechtext: Oh, no. Is the government undertaking to subsidize ferry boats ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I may say that this service was organized last year for the purpose of enabling the people of the whole district of Tadousac to have regular communication with the rest of the Dominion during the winter. Owing to the fact that the Saguenay river at its mouth, which is about two and a half or three miles across, from St. Catherines bay to Tadousac, is sometimes covered with ice, and that the north and east winds at that point are usually very strong, it is impossible for any but a strong boat to make the passage. Last year the government, in response to a petition from the people, organized a service, which gave complete satisfaction to the department and the public. Since then Price Bros., the proprietors of the boat, have organized a new company, and there has been some negotiation between the company and the government. The distance from St. Catherines bay to the wharf at Tadousac is nearly three miles.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: How are the mails eai'ried now?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: My hon. friend understands the situation. He knows that there is no bridge across the Saguenay until you reach Ha-Ha bay. a distance of sixty or seventy miles from the mouth; so that the people along the north shore of the St. Lawrence below Tadousac, if they want to come up to the settled parts of the north shore, when they reach Tadousac, have to travel inland sixty or seventy miles, and then come back and take the shore line up to Murray bay or the other inhabited portions of the country. This is intended to enable them to cross the mouth of the Saguenay river from Tadousac to St. Catherines bay, which is the great milling point of the Price Bros. This service has been performed by a little boat belonging to the Price Bros. They want to put another boat on. and they have formed a company for the purpose, and it is to enable that company to perform this ferry service that this subsidy is asked.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: That does not justify it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
I think it does. There is no bridge across the Saguenay
river and no way of crossing in the winter. There is no means of facilitating communication between those people at the mouth of the Saguenay and the upper part where they have no railway communication.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: This is purely a local affair, and should only be subsidized by the local government. Take the St. John river, which is quite as important as the Saguenay. It has a large population on both banks and yet there is no bridge from below Fredericton to St. John. There are ferries, but if these are subsidized at all they are subsidized by the provincial government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Not two minutes ago we voted a subsidy under identical conditions. We voted $3,000 to subsidize a line to carry passengers from the terminus of the railway at Paspediac down to Gaspd basin.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
That is the only way to give a regular service to the eastern part of the coast. The mail service has to cross the Saguenay during the winter and continue by land, and two years ago the mails were stuck on the west shore of the Saguenay for three weeks because the only means of crossing over was by canoe, and the wind was too strong. But with a small steamer you could have a regular service no matter what way the wind was.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
With reference to this vote from Tadousac into St. Catherines bay. and Tadousac, some facts have come to my knowledge since you left the Chair at six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, which put a rather different complexion on the resolution. This service is performed in summer by the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company. They receive a considerable grant for the service which is more important in summer than in winter. For some years, the winter carrying of the mails to the district below the Saguenay has become of importance because several new industries have started there. Last year there was a great delay in the conveyance of the mails-as much as eighteen days would elapse before the mail could get across from the western shore of the Saguenay and to Tadousac thence fifty miles by vehicle, &c., by dog-train to Matasliquan, and further to Belle Isle by any conveyance that offered. The Price Company have built a steamer at a cost of some $20,000 which, during the winter, conveys the mail regularly across the Saguenay to Tadousac and brings the mail back from the east. There are two trips across the opening of the river every day-it is not straight across the river, but

there is a distance of about three miles for a service between St. Catherines bay We pay not for the steam service but for the mails in the winter time, because delay would be detrimental to the industries and to the growing population on the eastern side of the river. There is no road from Tadousac to where a crossing can be effected, and in winter, there is no crossing possible, I am informed, for twelve leagues up the river-you must go that distance before you find a place where the river is frozen across. Under the circumstances, the sum of $2,000 paid to the Price Company seems reasonable enough. Of course, it is local enterprise and falls under the jurisdiction of the provincial parliament. But, as I understand it, this is a subsidy for mail service which interests the whole Dominion.
(Mr. FOWLER. The statement made in explanation of the item did not show that this was especially for a mail service. The committee is establishing the principle that these subsidies shall be given for ferries that are certainly within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature. If this government has so much money that it can afford this sort of thing, I can suggest a place where it can spend some of its surplus cash. Along the shore of the Bay of Fundy in a portion of the constituency I represent, there are towns that have no steam communication at all, and a subsidy might be given to a line of steamers to ply between St. John, which is our commercial metropolis in New Brunswick, and the ports along the Bay of Fundy, for instance, St. Martin's quite a flourishing town. Alma, in the county of Albert, Waterside and the town of Albert, and other towns lying along the coast. The steamer could run all the year round. These places are certainly deserving of consideration.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I think there is a difference. This subsidy is to enable the mails to be brought across the Saguenay river, which would be impossible otherwise except by going some forty or fifty miles up the river to a point of crossing-and on the eastern side there are no roads at all. In the cases referred to by my hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) I suppose the mails are brought overland. The mails are brought from Quebec in winter overland to the mouth of the Saguenay, the difficulty is such as I have mentioned.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
I thought it was said that there was a large business done by this ferry across the river, and that the country there was comparatively thickly settled. If that be so, one would expect to find that this boat had considerable earning capacity, enough to ensure a profit -without this subsidy. So far, this looks to me like some other cases we have had brought to our notice. A company running a steamboat asks for a subsidy with the idea that not much Mr. MONK.
inquiry will be made and that it will be a good thing to have. If there is a paying business, there is no need of this subsidy. But, if the subsidy is necessary to continue the service, and if there is no other way of carrying the mails, it would be much more likely to be justified.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: The representations that impressed the department were not primarily with regard to the mails. They regarded it as a commercial enterprise. Many of the steamers subsidized promote trade between ports of the Dominion which otherwise would not be readily accessible. The owners in this case were able to convince the minister that it was worth the amount of the vote to encourage the trade of the country, the mails being carried as a part of the contract. But the company now want $3,000 and refuse to take the contract for less. The department would not give the $3,000, and so there is no contract. The minister asking only $2,000, and is not prepared, I understand to give more.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Was there not a boat running there before the subsidy was given ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: There is a great deal in what my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) says. But, as a matter of fact, the boat performed this service last year for the first time. It was not generally known throughout the district that the boat would run regularly. There has been a considerable development of that region, and when the existence of this service is better known probably people will avail themselves more of it, and it will not be necessary to pay even $2,000 for the conveyance of the mails. The boat can carry six teams and a large number of passengers. It does a useful work generally in the gulf, I believe that last year it crossed from St. Catherines bay to Rimouski in the beginning of March. The Deputy Minister of Marine was on board on that occasion. But the traffic will probably develop, it is merely beginning.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
I want to argue this matter from a business standpoint as business men around this board. Now, is it a business subsidy or a mail subsidy ? The representation to the minister is that it is a business subsidy for the purpose of promoting trade. If you take it on that ground, all the precedents of this parliament are against giving what you may call a mere ferry subsidy. It is to all intents and circumstances a ferry, which stretches across a river in one of the provinces-a very useful and necessary convenience to have, but it is a thing which, in all the other provinces of the Dominion, has been kept up and subsidized, if at all, by the province. We have them all over New Brunswick. In my time, I re-

member numerous applications were made to bare these ferries subsidized. There was one particular ferry in my own county, running from St. John city three miles up to Bayswater, perhaps a little more. I well remember the deputations and pleas that were made to me to get a subsidy for that. The answer of the government always was, It is simply an internal ferry service ; it is entirely within a province, and the province itself must pay the subsidy ; and, as a matter of fact, the province always paid the subsidy, and pays it up to this day.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Does it carry the mails, too ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
Yes ; and they are paid by the Postmaster General, who pays for the conveyance of the mails of the country, and he pays for the mail bag that is carried on that boat a very small amount, a couple of hundreds dollars probably for the whole season. That is a legitimate payment for the carriage of mails. Then take the river St. John from its mouth up ; here and there you come across a ferry. The St. John river is a wide river, in some parts a mile and three-quarters, sometimes a mile and sometimes three-quarters of a mile, and there are ferries all along the river. Two ferries used always to run opposite Fredericton, the capital of the province, one running up the Nashwassis and the other across to the Nasliwalc, a distance, in the one case, of about two miles and, in the other, probably of three-quarters of a mile. Never have they asked for a subsidy for these ferries, and if anything was given to them it was given to them by the municipality or by the legislature. You And ferries along the St. John river all the way up. They are all treated in that way. There is a ferry in Nova Scotia, from Dartmouth to Halifax, kept up by the municipalities, and not by the Dominion government. So when you come to the matter of subsidizing ferries for commercial purposes, really it ought not be discussable in this chamber. Where are you going to stop if, under the shadow of a commercial subsidy, you are going to subsidize different ferries ? Now, another point was brought up, and it is one that ought to be looked at fairly. The mails are to be carried to the people on the other side of the river and they are to get their mails delivered on this side of the river. If there is need of a traverse there, and it is difficult in the winter to cross, that is the Postmaster General's business ; he has to see that the public are served with the mails, and if it is necessary to pay $1,000 to get that service, he must pay it. If it is necessary to pay more he must do it, because he is bound to keep up the postal service, and he is bound to dispense so much of the public money as is necessary in order to keep up that service. When this item first came up I took it as a commercial subsidy, and it did not seem to me that
it was admissible here at all. As a postal service it is quite admissible, but then it ought to go through the Postmaster General, and he ought to give what is generously sufficient in order to have the mails carried across.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
There is a great deal to be said in support of the views put forward by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster). But the conditions existing at this particular place are entirely different from those that exist in any other part of Canada. Take the whole north shore of the St. Lawrence, from Murray bay down to Labrador, and as soon as navigation is closed the people of that country are absolutely shut out from communication with the outside world, except by means of the road that passes along the shore of the St. Lawrence. Now, from St. Catherine's bay, on the west side of the mouth of the Saguenay, to Quebec, there are facilities for communication, no difficulty about that ; that is to say, you have a road by which you can get out, even though it takes three, or four, or five days, or a week, or a fortnight. in bad weather, to cover the distance. But from Tadousac down the full length of the north shore of the St. Lawrence, they are absolutely without any means of access to the outside world ; there is no boat, no railway, no means of communication whatever, except by this road which runs along the shore of the St. Lawrence river ; and when they reach Tadousac then they are obliged to go, I am sure, it must be sixty or seventy miles inland to get up to a point where they can cross the Saguenay river and get to the other side ; and after they have reached the west side of the Saguenay, they have to go down to S. Catherine's bay along the shore. As a commercial proposition, it does seem to me that it stands in line of all the subsidies that have been given in order to facilitate communication. We are constantly aiding railways, we are constantly aiding steamboat services. Why? In order to give facilities to enable people to communicate with the outside world. Now, the intention here is to enable these people to cross the river at that point and save 140 miles of carriage-that is practically what it amounts to. Now, there is no use in endeavouring to cover this thing up in any way ; it cannot be pretended it is merely a mail subsidy, because, after all, the government can have a mail service if it goes 140 miles as well as if it merely crosses the river. It seems to me it can be defended on the principle that it gives facilities to these people who are to the east of the mouth of the Saguenay river to go up to Quebec and have communication with the outside world. So far as the service itself is concerned, it is performed by a firm down there, as I remember it, who are interested to some extent in the commercial development of that part of the country,

the firm of Price Brothers. My hon. friend, I think, will agree that they are one of the most respectable firms in the province of Quebec.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: That does not enter into the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: But it shows this : these people contributed to that service for their own advantage, and I am informed by those who know that after having endeavoured to carry on that service, they find they cannot do it for the subsidy hitherto paid them. Notwithstanding all the business they get, notwithstanding the subsidy they have received, it is not a paying concern, and they cannot go further with it. Now, from the commercial standpoint, this service must drop if we do not help it. I think the fairest way is to state the facts to the House, and let the House decide what is to be done.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
Granting everything my hon. friend has said, which is no doubt the true ground, and that it would be a hardship to go sixty miles on one side to find a place to cross over and then sixty miles down on the other, what does it all amount to '! The whole point is the purpose for which the subsidy is paid. For instance, suppose there is a road which makes a long detour of sixty or eighty miles, suppose it is possible to get rid of a portion of this distance, making it probably one-third, one-eighth or one-tenth of the distance, but at the same time at greater cost, they don't come to the Dominion government and ask for that. It seems to me the whole point involved is the making of a traverse way in the province ; it is the same as a road, and it is the provincial government that has to see whether the road is the shortest and best to accommodate the people. Now, if that traverse is necessary, it is the duty of the provincial government to provide a roadway, a highway for its people, which is more convenient than the roundabout higli-wav. As it crosses the water, it becomes a ferry, and it is the provincial government, and not the Dominion government, which should supply it. The amount of money, involving only $2,000 or $3,000, is a mere bagatelle. It is not the amount, but it is some principle that I am now arguing for, and whilst I accept the premises of the argument of my hon. friend, at the same time I would say that the government which has the administration of affairs in the province of Quebec is bound to look after that, and to give to the people better and shorter means of traverse than they have at the present time. Then I go farther in reference to the mail carrying business, and if I were the Postmaster General I would give a fair, and even a generous amount for the mail carrying part of it. A commercial subsidy you cannot call it; it is a travel or mail convenience. It is not for the amount Mr. FITZPATRICK.
of merchandise that is to come and go that it is needed, but it is to put passengers across backwards and forwards and to take the mails backwards and forwards. That is the point of difference.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I do not like to subscribe unconditionally to the proposition that if this is to encourage and facilitate trade and commerce it is outside the purview of this parliament. On the contrary the encouragement of trade aud commerce, I think, comes distinctly within our jurisdiction. I am not aware that in the province of Quebec or in any other province any description of subsidies which would be an encouragement to trade and commerce would uot belong exclusively to our jurisdiction. I think the conditions there render trade and commerce more difficult without the assistance of this steamship and the parties interested properly apply to us for assistance. I see in the subsidies that we grant every year very considerable amounts for a steam service between St. Stephen, N.B., St. Croix river points, Deer Island, Campobello, the inner islands, Passamaquoddy bay and D'Etete or Black bay and also one between Port Mul-grave and Canso and Halifax and Canso. Are these amounts voted purely for mail service ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Or are they also for the encouragement of trade ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Yes, trade.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I only wish to point that out. 1 could understand my hon. friend's argument if it were merely a question of establishing ferries. Not only are ferries under the jurisdiction of the provincial authority, but when a bridge is to be built upon a river entirely within the province the authorities interested cannot look to us for assistance. But if you place it on this ground that there are 140 miles of road to be traversed in winter that trade is developing there and when you grant a subsidy to this steamship uot only on account of mail service but on account of trade and commerce of that distant locality I think it comes within our jurisdiction and that it does not belong to the provincial authorities.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
In connection with this question it has been a matter of interest to me for a great many years why we do this in the maritime provinces and do not do it in any other portion of the Dominion. If the principle is a proper one we have a right to apply it all over, I could bring to the attention of the hon. minister very many backward places on the Georgian bay where a small subsidy would secure communication by steamer regularly in the summer, whereas, at the present time, steamers only come in casually whenever there are special cargoes for 'them. In many places on the Georgian bay where they have practically

no roads and where they have to travel a long way from one settled village to another to get their mail it would be a great convenience if they could get a small subsidy- whether you call it a commercial subsidy or for the carriage of the mails it does not matter. I know that years and years ago such a subsidy was applied for but refused. So far as my knowledge goes there never was an instance in which it was given. I remember thirty-four or thirty-five, or thirty-six years ago that strong efforts were made to get some assistance from the Dominion of Canada to carry the mails or assist in establishing a route' where the trade that was offered would not pay for a regular boat supply, but they were not successful. I have often wondered why it was that these subsidies were granted for services on the Atlantic coast and refused for service in the heart of Ontario. I never could see why it was justified in one case and not in another. If it is justifiable in one case it should be justifiable in both, but while one is denied it the other gets it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
We have in Quebec a very large graving dock that is the property of the government. Mr. Geo. Davie has been for years past the proprietor of a large wrecking plant. At one time he was the owner of a wrecking steamer called the ' Lord Stanley.' He was in the habit of using this wrecking plant to salve vessels at any point in the St. Lawrence and at -times he has gone down as far as the United States with his plant. I might say that it is the only plant in Quebec and that it is considered the best wrecking plant in Canada. In consequence of his using his plant for the purpose of going out of the St. Lawrence at times wrecks have occurred which have resulted disastrously because the means to salve the vessels were not readily

accessible. Some four or five years ago tiie owners of vessels at Montreal applied to tlie government to see if arrangements could not be made with Mr. Davie to keep bis wrecking plant always available for wrecks in the St. Lawrence. Every one who is familiar with the conditions in the lower St. Lawrence understands the advantage to a wrecked vessel of a wrecking plant being abie to go to its assistance at the earliest possible moment. As a result of the negotiations then entered into between the government and the shipping people of Montreal, Mr. Davie sold the - Lord Stanley ' and bought the present ' Lord Strathcona,' which has cost him something in the neighbourhood of $125,000 or $130,000 ; the understanding being that he would get a boat of that calibre which is greater than he required at the time, to facilitate the work of wrecking in the St. Lawrence. He was to get this retainer, as the bon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has correctly described it, on the understanding that his wrecking plant must always remain at Quebec, so as to be available for any call that may arise in any part of the St. Lawrence, and the wrecking plant cannot leave the St. Lawrence without the consent of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It is to be always accessible for wrecks in the St. Lawrence.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I am not rising to object to this, but I would call attention to the unfairness of the treatment of one locality as compared with another. For many years there have been wrecking plants on the Georgian bay and at times there has been serious competition from American wrecking plants coming in there. Efforts have been made from time to time to get the government to put some restriction on these American plants coming in, because the company -who have their money invested in the Canadian plants were not earning enough to make them pay and yet what work there was was divided up with the Americans. They received no assistance from the government either by way of subsidy or by coasting trade regulations. They were obliged to stand on their own bottom and continue as long as they could. Why apply one principle to Quebec and another to Georgian bay ? If the principle is correct in the one instance it must be equally correct in the other, and in my judgment the argument for assistance is much stronger on behalf of the Georgian bay wrecking plants owing to the very much more scattered nature of the shipping there. I call attention to this because I notice that in many lines there seems to be a distinction drawn beween one part of the country and the other.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
This wrecking plant has been in existence for years. It was not necessary for this government or any other to grant a subsidy to this company to main-Mr. FITZPATRICK.
tain a wrecking plant. It was when Captain Leslie removed from Kingston and took his plant down the St. Lawrence, that it was found necessary to give a subsidy to the Davie Company, and there is where the unfairness of this comes in. Here is a failwrecking competition as between Leslie and Davie and in order to help Davie out he is given this subsidy of $10,000 a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: What happened to Leslie when he went to Newfoundland ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Wrecking is turned over to Davie and there is where the disadvantage to Leslie comes in. What are the government doing in addition to this ? By their treatment of Davie they are preventing that competition which vessels would have in the St. Lawrence by granting this $10,000 a year. It is unfair to Leslie who is in competition with Davie for the matter to be put in that position.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: In what respect did he enter into competition with Leslie ? We all know that there have been wrecks in the St. Lawrence from time immemorial. I venture to say that during the past 20 years Captain Leslie had never gone down beyond Montreal except once, when he went to Newfoundland, and I think he has regretted that trip ever since.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: A vessel man made the statement in this House that Captain Leslie did wrecking in the St. Lawrence, and very successfully, and I prefer taking the word of a vessel man even to that of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick).

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: If my hon. friend will take the responsibility of making that statement of course I accept it, but I make the statement with some knowledge of Quebec-and I have been connected with the mercantile life of Quebec for many years-I make the statement that Captain Leslie has never gone below Montreal to the assistance of a wreck except in one instance when he went to Newfoundland, and we all know what occurred then.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I am very glad that the minister made that statement. Possibly in a few days we shall see whether the statement of a vessel owner in this House or that of the Minister of Justice is correct.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
The question seems to me to be whether or not it is a fair commercial venture. Was there any difficulty about wrecking in the St. Lawrence before this subsidy was granted ? There are wrecking plants in the maritime provinces, possibly none of them quite so extensive as this, although some of them are very efficient as I happen to know by reason of hav ing been professionally engaged in connection with claims where their services were being valued. They have always existed without any subsidy so far as I know, but

1 am prepared to concede ttiat conditions may be different in the St. Lawrence. I would like to have information on tnat point.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
I think the venture was successful, in fact Mr. Davie is a very rich man, and I think he made all his money out of the wrecking plant except some that he made out of repairs which he made in his dry dock. The question as I understood it was whether or not we could keep that valuable wrecking plant for exclusive use in the St. Lawrence, as I understood it. Of course these negotiations were not carried on through me.
The question was not whether this was a good venture. I am quite satisfied that as far as Mr. Davie himself is concerned, he was prepared to go on doing his business as he did, free to go wherever he liked. But the special purpose of this retainer was to keep his apparatus exclusively for the St. Lawrence. I think the original subsidy or retainer was $5,000. I do not think Mr. Davie has ever approached the department on the subject. It has all been done through the underwriters and shipowners of Montreal. He decided that $5,000 was not sufficient, and it was increased, if I remember rightly, to $10,000. So far as Mr. Davie is concerned, it is simply a business agreement. He has to consider whether it would suit him better to keep his plant for the St. Lawrence for a retainer of $10,000, or to be free to go where he likes either on the St. Lawrence or on the Atlantic. For instance, one of the things that occurred was this, Mr. Davie has the most powerful tug on this side of the Atlantic, the ' Lord Strathcona,' which he was in the habit of using to tow ships from the St. Lawrence around to New York. That has not happened very often, but it has happened ; and my hon. friend the leader of the opposition will understand how profitable such work as that is. But Mr. Davie is now barred from doing work of that kind by this retainer. This boats must remain exclusively for use in the St. Lawrence. The only question is whether it is a good business proposition.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: The minister has a contract with Mr. Davie ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Does he know what the terms of the contract are ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I have sent for it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
Has the Department of Trade and Commerce any reports as to the actual work which has been done in the way of wrecking by Mr. Davie ? If it has not, does it not think it should have ? If you give a retainer to a lawyer, you want to know whether he does any business for you. If you give a retainer to Mr. Davie, it is given in order that he may devote himself to wrecking in a certain area. What track 31
has the Department of Trade and Commerce kept of his operations ? It should have a report of every wrecking operation in which he has been engaged, and should be able to make certain that he has fulfilled his contract and has not gone beyond the bounds within which his contract limits him. But the matter has another aspect to me. It is sometimes wise to ask what other countries do in this respect. Does the minister know whether in the United States or in Great Britain the government has ever considered it necessary to give a retainer to one particular wrecking firm in this way in order to get its services, and to bind it to a certain portion of the commercial wrecking area ? I doubt very much whether such a policy has been adopted by any other country. If it has not, there must have been some good reason, either that it was not necessary or that some ill-effects come from it. I can see easily what ill-effect will come fiom this arrangement. It will absolutely paralyze all private wrecking energy and enterprise in the St. Lawrence. The moment it is known that one firm has a retainer for doing wrecking in the St. Lawrence, no private firm will establish a wrecking plant, and every firm that is in the business will go out of it, knowing that the competition is unfair, and in a little while you will come down to a monopoly. What happens then V Just what is happening now. $5,000 was at first considered a sufficient retainer. A year or two afterwards double the amount was considered necessary. Go on for another year or two, and you have a call for $15,000 or $20,000. It works that way, because you put yourself absolutely in the power of one company. The very policy which the government has adopted with regard to dredging is a negative answer to this system. You say you cannot trust your dredging to corporate or individual enterprise, and you have to build your own dredges in order to be independent. You meet with still another difficulty. If the government has to give a retainer for wrecking in a great mart or channel like the St. Lawrence river, with many vessels and with a proportionate number of wrecks, what reason is there why the government should not come to the aid of equally or more dangerous coasts in British Columbia or in the maritime provinces where trade and commerce is imperilled every day in the year ? I venture to say that there is not a man in half a million in the Dominion who imagines that the government has gone the length of giving a retainer to one firm for a wrecking apparatus. If they did they would realize the injustice of it. I am not saying a word against the necessity of having a good wrecking apparatus ; but the question is whether the government should step in and paralyze the initiative of the individual and the corporation by retaining here and there some large firm to carry on the work of wrecking within a certain area. It strikes me that this matter is more



important than it has probably seemed to some of ns before we began to look into it and think about it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Of course, it has had the approval of the committee for several sessions. I think the argument of the hon. gentleman would be a very strong one if there were other companies that could be relied upon at all times to render help if help were needed. But I am informed that there is no wrecking company making any complaint with reference to this arrangement. It would be manifestly unfair to subsidize one firm when without a subsidy we could have competition from different firms; but in the position of affairs which is represented to me, in which we have the absolute benefit of having a very strong wrecking plant always available, and we get that by a subsidy without which we could not get a wrecking plant at all, the question for the committee to consider is whether in the public interest the subsidy should be continued. On the great lakes, to whieh reference has been made, there is competition. We have more that one wrecking plant and the Americans have their wrecking plants, and there is a certain degree of reciprocity. As to the other question of the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Foster) as to whether any other government is giving a subsidy under those conditions, I am not aware of it. The question will have to be judged on the points I have mentioned. Could you get what you have now without a subsidy and also what is desirable in the interests of shipping ? If you cannot, is it worth, in the general interests, the amount we pay in order to secure what we have ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: The hon. minister assumes, as justification for asking for this vote, that there is no competition in wrecking in the St. Lawrence river. He has allowed two or three items to stand, and i hope a few days will be allowed to elapse before they are taken up so that we may obtain information which will prove that there are other wrecking plants and other men willing to go into that line of business in the St. Lawrence. There are other wrecking plants whose owners consider this favouritism to Mr. Davie as unfair to them. Only a year ago very strong complaints were made by these men. The vessel men were asked to sign a petition asking that the Davie plant be subsidized for the purpose of assisting wrecks in the St. Lawrence and they signed it, but they did so very unwillingly and because they were in this unfortunate position that if a wreck took place, the Davies had a monopoly of the business. It is not fair to say there were no complaints, because here are complaints and serious ones. Capt. Leslie has good grounds for complaint and has complained, and the department is aware of the fact.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
I hope my hon. friend the Minister of Customs will allow this item to Mr. FOSTER.
stand. The amount is a large one, but it is not to that so much we are objecting as to the principle involved. We have no precise information from the hon. gentleman. What we do know is that this retaining of a wrecking plant is not practised anywhere else and I hardly think that my hon. friend's analogy between retaining a wrecking plant and giving a retainer to a lawyer has any bearing on the subject. We know that Mr. Davie has made a great deal of money in this business, but because he cannot tow boats around from Quebec to New York- and that seems a very extraordinary enterprise for him to embark upon-we are asked to give him a retainer. We have no information as to what has been the effect of this retaining of Mr. Davie. What did be do last year in return for his retainer ? We are given no account of what he did when asked to vote this amount. This item ought to come under the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and we ought to know exactly what Mr. Davie did last year and what prospects there are of his doing sufficient this year to justify this subsidy.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: What my hon. friend asks is not unreasonable. No doubt the Minister of Mairne and Fisheries will have full record of the wrecks that have taken place. I am told that the condition of the contract requiring this plant to be always available has been always complied with. We have certificates to that effect signed by the officers of the Customs Department, but in view of the statement made by the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Ingram), who spoke with apparent knowledge, I do not think we would be warranted in pressing this item until he has the opportunity of giving the facts to the committee, so that we may know fully in what position we are. We will, therefore, allow the item to stand.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: With regard to what the hon. minister has said as to reciprocity In the use of wrecking plants, I am not very familiar with the laws of the United States but I am under the impression that our wrecking vessels are not allowed to conduct salvage operations on the American Coast.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
I do not know what
the laws of the United States are on that point, but I know that the 'Stanley ' went around and towed vessels down' to New York.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is absolutely correct about that. There is no objection to her towing, but I would hardly think that this wrecking plant would be allowed to conduct salvage operations on the coast of the United States. So far as the maritime provinces are concerned, I do not think that it has done much on our coast. I know that it has on the coast of Newfoundland, and I know it has come into competition there with wrecking plants from the province of Nova Scotia. Another considera-

tion we should not lose sight of is that the granting of this subsidy undoubtedly tends to discourage individual enterprise, because those engaged in similar work in the maritime provinces could hardly be expected to compete on equal terms with a wrecking plant which gets an annual subsidy.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Would the hon. minister also give us the amount of salvage which Mr. Davie has received each year from the wrecking he has done ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I know for a fact that the Americans do not allow our Canadian wrecking plants to operate in their waters, because the wrecking plant that was for years in the Georgian bay applied to the Americans for reciprocal rights and were refused, although American wrecking plants can come to Canadian waters to attend to wrecks. Then this company contended that it would be unprofitable for them to keep up their plant unless something was done to assist them or to relieve them of the difficulties which they had to contend with owing to the American wrecking plants there. But nothing was done. It is the grant of assistance in one locality and its refusal in another that I think is wrong.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: If a certain amount of money is necessary to keep a wrecking plant on the St. Lawrence, that money should not be given in the shape of a subsidy to one concern. I am inclined to think it would be better for the government to promote competition between wrecking plants and, at the close of the year, to give the money to the company that has done the best service for the public, iifstead of establishing a monopoly as the government is now doing. Perhaps the minister would be prepared to express an opinion on that subject when the item is again up for consideration.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I will mention the matter to the minister.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I think it would be well to ask the minister also, why there is no retainer for Mr. Leslie. There was discussion of this subject on the 25th of July last, from which it appears that we only began paying the retainer to the present company after Mr. Leslie went down there. Speaking as a lawyer, I think if we retain Mr. Davie, we ought to retain Mr. Leslie also. He has done quite a lot of work there and stands in the same position as Mr. Davie' does.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Has he done a lot of work there ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: It appears so from the discussion of last year. Mr. Reid, who is well informed, and who is a shipowner, stated- and he was not contradicted by the Minister of Trade and Commerce-that Mr. Leslie had done a lot of work there.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Below Montreal ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
I believe so.

speechtext: About 27 miles, I am informed by a member who knows the locality.

Steam service during the year 1905-6 between Quebec and Natashquan, calling at ports and places along the northern shore ot River St. Lawrence between such terminals, $3,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: This service is performed by the steamship ' St. Lawrence,' with a tonnage of 532, and 300 net, and a speed of 10 knots per hour. It is a tri-monthly service, carrying the mails.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: What is the distance from Quebec to Natashquan ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Five hundred and thirty miles. Natashquan is a little below the eastern limit of Anticosti Island, on the north coast of the St. Lawrence. This boat calls at stated ports. Last year she performed three trips until somewhere at the end of October she got on the rocks, where she is now. She was the old ' Douro ' that used to run down there when she was owned by the Frasers. She was sold about two years ago, and was repaired and recast, and called the ' St. Lawrence.' maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I heard complaints about that service last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Yes ; they came near having a dreadful catastrophe at the time the vessel was wrecked. It was found she was not properly equipped.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Are this boat and the 'King Edward ' both subsidized ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
Yes. If there is any part of this country that ought to receive some attention it is the north shore Mr. PATERSON.
of the St. Lawrence. Many industries are being established on that shore all the way from Tadousac down to Blanc Sablon. I think there are at least, to my knowledge, a dozen industries down there now, pulp and timber. There is the Eastern Company, the Dobell, Beckett & Company, and other firms established on that shore, and they have absolutely no means of access except through these steamers. My hon. friend will remember the fishing industries they have down there on the Moisie river and below. If I could have my way I would subsidize two boats, and would endeavour to have a weekly service. You cannot meet the case with only one boat. I would have a weekly service, with two boats, and endeavour to make them comply with the terms of their contract.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Is there any clause in their contract which compels these boats to keep up their regular service ? A year or so ago, you will remember, the ' King Edward ' several times voluntarily abandoned its regular service in order to engage in profitable wrecking operations. I was on the north coast at the time, and I know it was a great inconvenience to the people of that section to have this steamer, on several occasions, abandon her trips entirely and leave the passengers, who had been planning to take her, for several weeks in out-of-the-way places.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Years ago numbers of people on the lower St. Lawrence used to come up to Quebec to purchase their winter supplies towards the end of the season. On one occasion, because the owners of the ' King Edward ' thought the weather was not favourable they said they would not go down, and it was necessary for the government to interfere and get one of the government steamers to take these people back. That happened two years ago last autumn. I think that shore ought to be attended to properly, and my view would be that we should have a proper service, and to have that two boats at least would be required.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: My first question was whether the government, in return for the subsidies, were requiring the Holliday Brothers, who were the owners of the ' King Edward,' to make three trips regularly according to the schedule.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I think it requires they shall make a certain number of trips, but it does not fix the dates of sailing. That is where the inconvenience comes in. As long as they make two trips monthly, it is immaterial what date they select for start-ng.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
I agree that that service should be fully carried out. I understood the minister to say that that boat was badly equipped. Surely, if this government subsidizes boats, they ought to see that they

are properly inspected before the subsidy is paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
I do not want to speak in criticism, but it seems to me time to take some steps in this country to prevent such terrible disasters as that which took place on the ' Slocum ' in New York. Certainly, from information of some of my firiends who were on board the ' St. Lawrence ' when she was wrecked, the vessel was not equipped as she ought to have been.
I make the statement, not in criticism of my colleagues, as, of course, nothing of the sort is intended, but simply because I think that perhaps the officials ought to be notified of the necessity of looking after these vessels and seeing to it that they have all the requirements that the law makes necessary.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Would it not be an easy matter to make it a rule that no subsidy shall be granted to any vessel until it is thoroughly inspected?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: That is implied.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: It is implied but evidently in this case it has not been carried out.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I do not think it has been definitely stated yet whether that vessel got her" full subsidy. It seems to have been fully stated here to-night that she did not do her work, that she actually abandoned her voyage and went in for salvage. Has the money been paid yet?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Not yet.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: That is still being held back?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: So I am told. You are discussing the St. Lawrence ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: That was two years ago.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Well I want to know whether she got her subsidy or not. It is the 'King Edward' that I am referring to.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I am told that the claim was that they did their work between trips. The subsidy was earned and it was paid. I understood the bon. minister was talking about the St. Lawrence when I made my previous statement.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Is it not a fact that the Department of Marine and Fisheries makes a careful inspection of all passenger vessels that ply in our waters?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: The law requires them to do so.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.

speechtext:
Elder-Dempster & Co.
Montreal, Feb. 4, 1905.
F. C. T. O'Hara, Esq.,
Acting Deputy Minister,
Department of Trade and Commerce, Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Mr. O'Hara,-I am to-day in receipt of yours of the 3rd instant re cargoes carried by the South African steamers, for six months ending, we will say, with the February steamer, which is to sail on or about the 18th instant. We are including this steamer as we have her now practically fully booked.
The six months commencing with September, 1903, and ending with February, 1904. The steamers of the joint service, during this period carried practically full cargoes. A large proportion of the cargoes were composed of Canadian wheat and flour. We also had large shipments of Canadian lumber, more particularly red pine, and a fair quantity of manufactured Canadian goods, such as furniture, carriages, agricultural implements, ploughs, &c. We also had considerable shipments of Quaker oats, manufactured at Peterborough, Ont., also considerable metallic roofing. In the refrigerators of our steamers we had very heavy shipments of mild cured bacon, shipped by the Laing Packing and Provision [Company, Montreal, about 300 tons for each departure. We also had during October and November several thousand barrels of apples.
From September, 1904, to February, 1905. The steamer that sailed in September carried about three-quarters of a cargo, about sixty per cent being Canadian and forty per cent American. Owing to the contract by the Laing Packing Company with the Imperial Cold Storage Company, of Cape Town, having expired, the refrigerators carried a much smaller quantity of Canadian products than went in the same month in 1903. The steamer that sailed in October was a full ship, she had in her refrigerator equal to about 3,000 barrels of Canadian apples. Her cargo wrns composed principally of Canadian flour, considerably planed pine lumber, and manufactured lumber, such as doors, sashes, &c. The steamer that sailed in November, which was the steamship * Melville ' was about three-quarters full. Her cargo was composed of about fifty per cent of manufactured goods of Canadian origin and fifty per cent of American. The next steamer was the ' Etolia ' which sailed in December. This steamer carried practically a full cargo. Since her departure a decided improvement has taken place in the South African business, the financial position appears to have considerably changed, and in consequence the ' Wyandotte,' which sailed the end of January, had a very large cargo, and

sailed a full ship. She only took sufficient coal for the voyage to South Africa. Besides a large quantity of miscellaneous cargo, she had about 55,000 sacks of Canadian flour, but we are sorry to say she had very little refrigerator goods. The next departure will be the steamship * Melville ' in February. This steamer is fully booked. Her cargo will be largely composed of flour, practically eighty per cent' Canadian. At the present time we have secured about 55,000 sacks of flour, and about 200,000 feet of planed white pine, and about 20 cars of Quaker oats made at Peterborough, Ont.
Owing to better trade conditions in South Africa a decided improvement has taken place fh the demand, and our South African agent advises us that the corner has now been turned and that a continuance is expected. We are also advised that the preference is materially helping the importation of 'Canadian goods.
I am,
Yours very truly,
