speechtext: X concur in Xiis eonculding remark; I think that there will be a great advantage. We have now a preference in South Africa, our freight rates will be as low as those from the United States and with the preference, if we maintain the quality of our goods, the trade should greatly increase. Repeat orders are evidently being received now according to this statement as to flour and other items. In my own business my anxiety is not to make first sales, but to secure repeat orders. If you receive the repeat orders you know you have your customer, and as there are repeat orders coming in here I am led to believe that our people are sending goods there that will command the market if they once get a foothold and the preference I consider will be of so much advantage to us that it will turn the trade in our favour as against our American friends. I fully look for that and it will be very gratifying.

speechtext:
I scarcely think that is fair-, when we have to pay the subsidy, and the United States pay nothing. That

is giving the Americans a preference over the Canadians. I think they should pay something additional in order to make up for our subsidy. It is quite proper that Canadians should get the preference ; but if Americans want to ship goods in our subsidized vessels, surely they should pay some premium for the privilege. We assume that we get lower rates because of the subsidy we pay.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: When this contract was being made, if we had insisted that the vessels should be restricted to take Canadian goods alone, the probability is that no contract of this nature would have been made. The Canadian trade had to be almost created, but Canadian goods get the preference.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: When this subsidy was first granted, I understood that our vessels did call at American ports and take on American products of a similar character to our own, and carried them to South Africa In the vesesls that we subsidized, and placed them on the same market on which we put our goods. I scarcely think it is fair to our Canadian producers that we should subsidize vessels to carry American products to the very 'markets we want to get. I would rather give a larger subsidy and leave the American goods at home, and let our own goods get all the market. I do not think for a moment that we should carry American goods to be sold in competition with our own, and certainly not to enhance the price that we get for our goods, but rather to depreciate the price. It seems to me the Minister of Trade and Commerce should give this matter a little more consideration to make it fair to Canadians.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Should not the hon. gentleman give it a little more consideration ? Suppose a steamer were sailing with half a cargo of Canadian goods, and were consequently forced to charge a certain rate. If it could get another half cargo, which would enable it to reduce the rate correspondingly, would that not be an advantage to the Canadian shipper? The hon. gentleman must remember that the American is not the only competitor the Canadian Shipper has in the market. He has to meet English and German competitors as well. What we should have is a preference for Canadian goods and that is secured to us. The contract is a very good one for Canadian producers and I anticipate that we are going to do a large trade with South Africa.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
I was under the impression, when the subsidy was first granted, that our vessels called at American ports, but I may possibly have been mistaken. I think the principle all wrong of subsidizing vessels to carry American goods to a market we want to supply. It would Mr. HENDERSON.
be better for our producers to pay a little more freight and not have this competition. It may be that the United States goods which are shipped alongside of ours in the same vessel will be goods that will come into competition with ours, and a small fraction of difference in freight would not compare with the loss that may be sustained through this competition. For instance, apples may be sent from the United States as well as from Canada, we may also have American cheese sent in these same vessels which carry Canadian cheese, and these may depreciate the Canadian goods. It may be that in this way we will be depressing the market to the injury of my hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Maclaren), who, I understand, ships cheese to a large extent from Canada to South Africa and even to Mexico. We heard the Postmaster General describing the large amount of cheese he saw inthat latter country. I trust that the subsidy to be paid vessels running to Mexico will not be paid to vessels which call at American ports and which will carry American cheese and thus lower the price in that market of the cheese which the hon. member for North Perth is sending there. I would like him to get the very best prices possible, and a slight reduction in freight, consequent upon the vessel carrying American cheese, would not compensate him for the loss that would result from this competition.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: My hon. friend must remember that American goods shipped in American bottoms might be of the same class as the Canadian goods shipped in these subsidized vessels, and we would not really have the market exclusively to ourselves in any case. The Americans are not limited to shipping by this line, but I think that we will be found in this position, that the cheese shipped by the hon. member for North Perth will be found superior to anything the Americans can send, and I have no doubt that we will be in a similar position as regards other lines. ,

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
I quite agree with the hon. minister that our Canadian cheese is superior to the American. That is the reputation it has in the old country, and no doubt it will have the same reputation in the South African market, but there is this danger that the inferior cheese will be quoted against our better cheese, and the South Africans may not at first be able to discriminate between the two. But if the cheese and other products of the United States can be sent in American vessels, why do they send them to Canada to be shipped by our vessels? We are subsidizing vessels to carry American products. The Americans do not seem to have a line of steamers from New York to South Africa which will carry freight as cheaply as ours, and I am still of the opinion we should not

encourage that American trade in our bottoms. Even suppose there should be ten per cent of the space not filled up, this company which is getting the subsidy ought to be still prepared to give us a fair rate.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Canadian freight has the preference over American freight, but the question is whether it would not be in the interest of Canada to allow these vessels to complete their cargo with American goods rather than to go with only a part cargo. There is this other point, that the preference which has been granted to us in South Africa will be very advantageous, not only in the way of preference, but also in the way of determining what are Canadian goods. I look to great benefit from the preferential arrangements we have made with South Africa. I think it was generous on their part to enter into such an arrangement, for it looks as if, in the course of trade, we may hope to do a larger trade with them than they can hope to do with us.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.

This is a very important point that the hon. member for Queen's
(Mr. A. Martin) has raised. When we give this large subsidy there certainly should be no discrimination against Canadian trade. I do not say that there is anything improper in vessels subsidized by Canada carrying American freight. We want to carry the trade of the world, if we can, but we must not pay a subsidy and allow those who enjoy it to discriminate against our own people.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Hon. gentlemen who have spoken on this subject have only raised the fringe of a very important question, which applies not only to steamships, but to the railways that we have so heavily subsidized. Of the thousand millions invested in Canadian railways, over one-quarter came from the people of Canada. And to-day the Department of Railways, this government, and the Railway Commission, allow these great roads to carry traffic of the United States that competes with our products in the old country through Canada at about one-half what the Canadian farmer has to pay. The wheat of the western states, the corn of Illinois, go through Canada to the sea-board for one-half what is charged for carrying Canadian grain. I have no doubt steamship companies fill this up with American cargo at lower rates than they give Canadian goods-that is a practice of all transportation companies whether by sea or land. There is only one cure and that is that Canadian and steamship services should be used altogether for the interest of the Canadian public.

speechtext: The minister should come to parliament and present a statement, giving the total grant, in what direction trade is improving, or otherwise, what our agents abroad have to report, and so on. He could present it in a brief form that would go to the public and be of public use. I shall look for better things next year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Do I understand from the hon. gentleman that he considers this valuable report not worth studying, and that he cannot find what he is seeking ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: The Minister of Finance, in his budget speech of an hour, gives the country an intelligent view of its financial affairs, and that is something that ought to be done by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in bringing down his estimates.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I could not undertake to give a list of all the different cargoes that came from South Africa here and that went there from Canada-of course, I can give you the round numbers, but I cannot be expected to give more. We ought to be able to give you the amount of the return cargoes in bulk, and perhaps in a general way what they consist of. But to go into all the details on the estimates could not be expected, especially when you have reports prepared already giving them. Might I ask the hon. gentleman to read the Trade and Commerce report, and if there is anything that he does not find in it and that he wants to know, I will try and supply the lack.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman refer ns to the page of that valuable work where we will find about the return cargoes?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
In the return of the commercial agencies. The conditions of trade between the two countries are such that we may hope to benefit more by this reciprocal arrangement and by these steamship subsidies than our fellow-colonists will. They are not in a position to send ns as much as we are able to send them, but they are going to be a profitable market for us. We are doing what we can to encourage trade.
Administration of the Chinese Immigration Act, including remuneration to Trade and Commerce and Customs officers, $4,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: It is the same vote as last year. The effect of the Chinese capitation tax is that there was collected during the calendar year of 1904 $3,200. This includes an amount of $1,700, being a $100 tax collected on seventeen Chinamen who had entered previous to January 1st, 1904. But the tax was not collected at all after that date. The remaining $1,500 is made up of a tax of $500 paid by the Canadian Pacific Railway on each of three Chinamen who had deserted. That is, as I understand, seventeen Chinamen had entered under the previous rate. No Chinese have paid the $500 tax under the new Act.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Have none come in ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: There were these three deserters. But outside of them, no Chinamen landed except fifty-six exempted ones. Under the law merchants, professional men, students and men of science are exempted.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: How is that $4,000 you are asking for to be spent ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: In paying the salaries of the collectors of customs, inspectors and interpreters.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: How much was spent last year ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Salaries, $3,953.31 ; contingencies, $239.95.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: How many officials are there ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: The number of officers is not here. The deputy says there are six.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Are these special officers ?	.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: No, they are officers of customs. Though the Chinese portion of the administration is directed by the Department of Trade and Commerce, they make use of the Canadian customs. We do not pay the inspectors.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. minister if these officers are preventive officers for
the purpose of seeing that the law of exclusion is rigidly enforced ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Yes, though they are customs officers they act under the Department of Trade and Commerce in reference to the Chinese.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I understand that the flow of Chinese into this country has absolutely ceased.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: It looks like it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Not a single one came in last year since the tax of $500 was imposed ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Then is it necessary to pay $400 for these officers when Chinese immigration has absolutely ceased ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: The influx might be renewed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Do the hon. minister and the government ask us to accept the idea that the Chinese are being excluded ? I can only speak from what 1 observe in Toronto and 1 think I can say without fear of contradiction that the Chinese portion of that city has increased by 1,000 or 2,000 within the last year or so, and that we have probably 5,000 of them there. I do not know what the Chinese population is in Montreal but they are coming into eastern Canada at a surprising rate. They are enterprising people to a large extent. They are going into business more and more in Toronto with the result that in some streets every third or fourth shop is a Chinese store. They all say that they come from British Columbia and that they have been in the country for some time, but I think these officers who have charge of this department are not keeping their eyes open. They cannot come from the United States because they have to pay more to get into that country, but the number of Chinamen who are coming into the eastern portion of Canada is something surprising, and it will be interesting if anybody cares to investigate to try and find out where they are coming from.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: They are coming from P.ritish Columbia. Having come in once they are at liberty to come east.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I know that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I understand my hon. friend to say that they are going into business. They must know the English language to do that and therefore they must have been in the country for some time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Some of them know very little of it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: How many came in last year ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: None.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Chinese ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Came in ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Certainly. I advise the hon. minister to read the Trade and Commerce Report.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I am afraid it does not give that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Look at page 750. The total collections were $474,420. The revenue that the provinces got is a very large revenue. It amounts to $231,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: The explanation of that must be that knowing that the tax was to be increased there was an extra rush into the country at that time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: My hon. friend is a most versatile man.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: That is the fact because none have come in since.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: The hon. minister gave all these reasons why none came in and now he gives another reason why 4,719 came in.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: It was owing to the fact that they knew that there was to be a raise from $100 to $500 and the Chinamen were sharp enough to get in before the tax of $500 came into effect, while those who did not get in are evidently staying away from us.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I ask the hon. gentleman to take a little of the advice he gave to my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) and just take a square hour and read over his own report.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: That is not my report. I have hardly as much spare time as my hon. friend, but he has given me convincing proof of what I have said that all the information he seeks for he can get if he only looks for it. He has set me right in reference to that matter and I have no doubt that if he pursues his investigations further he would be able to answer my hon. friend from South York.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I think the British Columbia newspapers will support the statement made by my hon. friend from South York. They charge that Chinese are entering Canada in the eastern portion of Canada. We have also the statement made by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Smith) who quoted the ' Nanaimo Free Press ' to the effect that Chinamen were entering Canada and that some of them were even accompanied by a special officer of the department. The impression seems to be that the Chinamen are coming into Canada in the eastern portion of Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
I can hardly let the statement the hon. member for North Mr. PATERSON.
Toronto (Mr. Foster) has made that 4,719 Chinamen came into the country last year pass without saying a word or two in regard to it. If the Trade and Commerce report shows that for the whole of the year 1904 a certain number of Chinamen came in that statement must apply to the year ending the first of January, 1904.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I can only take the report and I must take it as being authentic. The report tells me that up to the 30th June, 1904, for the year 1904 there were 128 exempted, 4,719 paid fees and there were these collections, refunds and the like of that. There is no doubt about that information. How many have come in since 30th of June, 1904, up to last of the calendar year I do not know.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I would point out to my hon. friend from North Toronto that since the imposition of the tax there have been no Chinamen coming into this country with the exception of the few who are specially exempted.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: When did the tax become operative ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: On the first of January.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: 1904. The tax has been in vogue for the past year. Chinamen have not been coming in. I would tell my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean} that if Chinamen are coming into eastern Canada we are very pleased to know it, as they must be coming from British Columbia. We had the scourge long enough with us. They are not now coming into British Columbia. We suffered very severely from the great horde of Chinamen coining into the country and the tax has been a splendid thing as far as British Columbia is concerned. You are now getting them and you will find very shortly that you will have the people rising up and demanding that they shall be shut out.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: But the dumping clause cannot apply to Ontario.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Well I suppose that you have lots of Chinamen in Ontario who do not wear long queues.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
I do not see how it is that these books do not agree. The Department of the Interior has charge of immigration. It gives a list of the immigrants that come in, but I do not find any Chinamen in the list while in the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce my hon. friend from North Toronto has found the record of a very large number of Chinamen.
In addition to that I asked the minister some time ago for the number of preventive officers he had employed, and he did not

give us that information. I think before the item is passed he should give the number of preventive officers and try to make some explanation. The reports with reference to immigration ought all to agree. I do not see why the Department of the Interior should get one report and the Department of Trade and Commerce another. I have asked the minister to give the number of officers who are employed to prevent Chinamen coming into this country and he does not see fit to answer.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I am sorry the hon. gentleman understood that I would not answer. I was trying to get the information that would enable me to answer him satisfactorily. I am told that there are six special officers who are under the Department of Trade and Commerce, but all the customs officers have the circulars and know the regulations with reference to Chinese and it is part of their duty to see that no Chinaman shall enter without paying the capitation tax. But they are officers of customs. The deputy tells me that there are six interpreters and officers especially charged with this duty who are under the pay of the Department of Trade and Commerce.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Will the minister tell us the pay that each of these officers receives ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: I have not it here, but if we had the Auditor General's Report we would find it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Supposing that a Chinaman comes from China, lands at Vancouver, and is passing through Canada to Newfoundland accompanied by a special officer. Would he give bonds ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Oh, yes, he would be under bonds.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext: Supposing that he passed through Newfoundland and in the course of a year or so entered Canada could he not get over the tax in that way.

maintopic: SUPPLY-FREE TRANSPORTATION OF HAY ON I.C.R.
speechtext:
No.
Some resolutions reported.
On motion of Mr. Paterson, House adjourned at 10.40 p.m.

Tuesday, February 14, 1905.
